EU and India conclude negotiations on EUR 93.5 billion Horizon Europe Programme The European Commission and India have successfully concluded negotiations on India’s association with Horizon Europe, the European Union's EUR 93.5 billion flagship research and innovation initiative. ANI | Updated: 06-11-2026 19:05 IST | Created: 06-11-2026 19:05 IST

Representative Image (Photo/Reuters). Image Credit: ANI

SHARE

Key Takeaways AI Summary

Analyzing article...

The European Commission and India have successfully concluded negotiations on India’s association with Horizon Europe, the European Union's EUR 93.5 billion key funding programme for research and innovation. The agreement marks a milestone in EU-India relations, strengthening scientific cooperation, opening new opportunities for research, and deepening the bilateral strategic partnership. Once signed and ratified by both sides, the association is envisaged to take effect in January 2027, the European Commission stated. Under the agreement, researchers, businesses, and research organisations in India will be eligible to receive funding directly from Horizon Europe and lead collaborative projects under Pillar II: 'Global Challenges and European Industrial Competitiveness'. As the largest segment of the programme, Pillar II finances multi-national research tackling major societal and technological issues, including health, digital, industry, space, climate, energy, and the bioeconomy. Welcoming the development, Ekaterina Zaharieva, EU Commissioner for Startups, Research and Innovation, highlighted the mutual economic and scientific benefits of the landmark deal. "The agreement opens new opportunities for our businesses," Zaharieva said. "Horizon Europe will help our researchers and innovators work together on what comes next. We want Europe and India to be partners in developing the technologies that will shape our future." Association represents the closest form of cooperation offered by the EU to non-EU nations under Horizon Europe, allowing organisations from associated countries to participate on equal terms with their EU counterparts in covered areas in exchange for financial contributions to the programme's budget. The conclusion of negotiations follows exploratory talks launched on February 6, 2026, and formal negotiations initiated on July 17, 2026. Bilateral scientific cooperation between the two sides builds on the Agreement for Scientific and Technological Cooperation—originally signed in 2001 and renewed until 2030—as well as the Joint EU–India Comprehensive Strategic Agenda towards 2030, adopted at the EU–India Summit on January 27, 2026. Technological collaboration has also expanded through the EU–India Trade and Technology Council, focusing on key digital domains such as artificial intelligence, digital public infrastructure, semiconductors, high-performance computing, digital skills, and 6G telecommunications. Further facilitating mobility in the ICT sector, the first European Legal Gateway Office in India was launched last February. Running from 2021 to 2027, Horizon Europe currently includes 23 associated non-EU countries, ranging from the United Kingdom, Canada, and Japan to South Korea and Switzerland. Negotiations were also recently concluded with Australia, with an agreement expected to be signed shortly. Through this, Indian institutions would receive grants directly from the European Commission, Indian scientists could lead and coordinate massive international research consortia and India would participate in the program on the same terms as EU Member States, in exchange for a fair financial contribution to the program's budget. (ANI)

SHARE

Key Takeaways AI Summary

Analyzing article...

The death toll from Russia's bombing of an aid distribution point in Ukraine's southeastern Zaporizhzhia region on Monday has risen to 53, the acting regional governor said on Friday, making it one of the deadliest strikes on civilians this year. In a post on the Telegram messaging app, Mykhailo Semikin said search and rescue work at the site in the village of Komyshuvakha had entered its fifth day. Ukraine's Emergency Service had earlier said the toll was 50 and that search and rescue work was continuing despite difficult conditions and the constant threat of repeat Russian strikes.

item.title: Trump questions Russian fuel ban, signals no change
item.description: President Donald Trump questioned the US law banning Russian petroleum imports, stating he would review it, though no policy change was announced amid a dispute over his administration's authorisation ...
item.content:encoded:
Trump questions Russian fuel ban, signals no change President Donald Trump questioned the US law banning Russian petroleum imports, stating he would review it, though no policy change was announced amid a dispute over his administration's authorisation of Russian diesel transactions. ANI | Updated: 06-11-2026 10:05 IST | Created: 06-11-2026 10:05 IST

US President Donald Trump (Photo/Reuters). Image Credit: ANI

SHARE

Key Takeaways AI Summary

Analyzing article...

President Donald Trump has cast doubt on the US law banning Russian petroleum imports, indicating that he would review the legislation while declaring no policy change amid mounting controversy surrounding his administration’s clearance of Russian diesel transactions. “That probably makes it a pretty bad law. I'll take a look at it, sure,” Trump stated after a journalist informed him that the measure had been enacted by Congress and signed by President Joe Biden in 2022. During his interaction in the Oval Office, the reporter raised questions regarding a vessel transporting Russian diesel across the ocean towards the United States, alongside the legal restrictions governing the offloading of its cargo. Initially, Trump questioned whether the restriction fell under the purview of the Jones Act, prompting the correspondent to clarify that the issue pertained to legislation passed in 2022. His response provided no timeline, proposed amendment or explanation regarding how the administration intended to reconcile its authorisation of diesel imports with the statutory import prohibition, nor did he declare that the ban had been lifted. This distinction remains critical, given that the Treasury had previously granted a separate authorisation roughly four weeks earlier. On October 9, the Office of Foreign Assets Control released General License 135, permitting financial dealings otherwise prohibited under two sets of Russia-related sanctions regulations whenever they involve the sale, delivery, offloading or importation of Russian-origin diesel. The document explicitly covers imports into the United States, with the waiver remaining in effect until 12.01 am Eastern Daylight Time on April 7, 2027. While exempting withdrawals from accounts maintained at US financial institutions belonging to Russia's central bank, National Wealth Fund or Finance Ministry, the licence specifically targets diesel rather than signalling a general reopening of trade encompassing all Russian petroleum products. Conversely, the Ending Importation of Russian Oil Act, formally approved on April 8, 2022, independently prohibits inbound shipments of Russian products listed under Chapter 27 of the US tariff schedule. The framework outlines a strict protocol for lifting this restriction, requiring presidential certification verifying an agreement accepted by Ukraine regarding Russia's withdrawal and a halt to hostilities, the elimination of any immediate Russian military threat directed at NATO members, and recognition of Ukrainian self-determination. Additionally, the requirement necessitates prior consultation with congressional committees, alongside a 90-day review period following certification before any cancellation takes effect, unless Congress passes a resolution of disapproval. The aforementioned Treasury licence, on its own, does not establish that this statutory process has been fulfilled. New Jersey Governor Mikie Sherrill formally contested the approval through a November 2 letter addressed to port and terminal operators, just three days before Trump's recent comments. “The Trump Administration’s authorisation of Russian fuel imports directly conflicts with federal law,” she asserted. Sherrill contended that the legislation did not grant the executive branch blanket authority to set aside the prohibition through licences, cautioning commercial entities against accepting deliveries of the petroleum and vowing that New Jersey would deploy all available legal and regulatory measures to block such imports. (ANI)
